entries.title: Large crowd causes Lake Shore Drive closure at 57th Street
entries.summary: <p>A portion of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive was closed Monday night after large crowds caused a heavy police presence in Jackson Park.</p><p>Traffic was closed around 9 p.m. on Lake Shore Drive at 57th Street, Chicago police said.</p><p>Around 1,000 people were seen gathered in the area, some jumping on top of cars. A few people in the crowd were seen throwing objects, and others charged toward a line of police officers.</p><p>No arrests were reported. The crowd size had dwindled by 10 p.m. </p><p>On Friday, University of Chicago Police issued an alert about a possible “teen takeover” gathering that had been planned for Monday night near 57th Street Beach.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a40000" name="image-a40000"></a> <picture entries.title: Benefits of Bears’ megaproject bill ‘murky’ at best for Illinois taxpayers: Cook County treasurer analysis
entries.summary: <p>Proposed property tax incentive legislation intended to keep the Chicago Bears from moving to Indiana might maintain local pride, but perhaps not at a price that’s worth it for the average Illinois homeowner, a new report from Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ office suggests.</p><p>The benefits are “clear” for big companies like the Bears but “murky” for most taxpayers, according to a 12-page analysis released Tuesday that steers clear of policy recommendations but offers plenty of reason for skepticism around the megaprojects bill being haggled over in Springfield.</p><p>“Megaproject property tax savings could total billions of dollars — money that would otherwise go to fund schools and other local governments,” the report says.</p><p>“Huge real estate projects can create jobs, boost sales tax revenue and provide other benefits to their surrounding communities. But property tax breaks for megaprojects would for decades severely limit one key goal of economic development: expansion of the property tax base that provides relief to other taxpayers who get no tax certainty,” it says.</p><p>Pappas’ report evaluates the bill that passed the Illinois House last month but will need major changes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/21/bears-stadium-megaprojects-bill-arlington-heights-obstacles-brandon-johnson-jb-pritzker-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>to have any hope of passing</u></a> the Illinois Senate before the spring legislative session concludes. Lawmakers have until midnight Sunday to get a bill to the end zone.</p><p>Researchers from the treasurer’s office looked broadly at the megaprojects concept that Gov. JB Pritzker has long championed outside the context of the Bears’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>stadium saga</u></a>. Dozens of other states have such laws in place that allow companies to negotiate discounted payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) instead of their full property tax bills to local taxing bodies, as long as they’re investing in massive developments.</p><p>Such incentives “would have significant economic effects well beyond the northwest suburbs,” Pappas’ researchers found, noting five Chicago developments under construction last year that reached the $100 million threshold for the potential tax breaks.</p><p>While there’s no comparable property in the state, Pappas’ office estimated the Bears would be on the hook for a $53.2 million property tax bill on an Arlington Heights dome, if assessed at a conservative $675 million market value.</p><p>Freezing the current bill of less than $4 million on the Arlington Heights site plus a hypothetical $10 million PILOT, Pappas’ office estimated the team would get “an annual tax break of more than $39 million — or more than $1.5 billion over 40 years.”</p><p>By comparison, Old Orchard Mall in Skokie paid a $17.6 million bill in 2024 while producing a bigger economic impact than a stadium would, according to Pappas’ office.</p><p>“[F]or many Chicagoans, the Bears are an iconic presence, some might say as much an emblem of the city as Willis Tower,” <a class="Link" href="http://www.cookcountytreasurer.com/pappasportalnewsletter.aspx?newsletterid=2026052601" target="_blank" ><u>the report says</u></a>. “Willis Tower paid $50 million in property taxes in 2024.”</p><p>The team has pegged their potential tax bill beyond $150 million, which they say makes it financially infeasible for them to remain in Illinois as they’ve narrowed their choices to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/11/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-what-to-know" target="_blank" ><u>Arlington Heights and Hammond</u></a>.</p><p>Indiana lawmakers are trying to lure the team to Hammond with a significantly sweeter taxpayer-funded deal for the Bears, who have committed to covering $2 billion <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/18/bears-nfl-stadium-sites-arlington-heights-hammond-not-hammond-nfl-quarterly-meeting-orlando-tuesday" target="_blank" ><u>wherever they end up breaking ground</u></a>.</p><p>Pappas’ office suggested a Hoosier dome that’s closer to downtown Chicago than Arlington Heights is wouldn’t be the end of the world.</p><p>“[A] stadium in Hammond would still produce economic benefits for Chicago and the state of Illinois — with Indiana taxpayers picking up the $1 billion tab to subsidize the development,” the report says. “And the team would still be named the Chicago Bears, so bragging rights would still be intact for the Chicago area just as they are for New York City even though the New York Giants and New York Jets play in New Jersey.”</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is making a late push in Springfield to scuttle the Bears’ path out of Soldier Field. Pappas has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/18/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-mayoral-campaign-chicago-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>said she’ll run for mayor</u></a> next year.</p><p>Her office questioned whether discounted taxes and PILOT payments made by developers would “be enough to cover the increased costs of education and other local services made necessary by their projects.”</p><p>“The bill does include provisions that require projections of resulting additional costs to schools and mandates that districts be compensated, but there is nothing that guarantees similar analysis of impacts on non-school government services, such as new infrastructure, police and fire protection, trash pickup and inspections,” the report says. It cites the extensive catalog of academic studies that have determined public subsidies for stadiums are generally raw deals for taxpayers.</p><p>“If the frozen payment and special payment are not high enough to fund those added services, other taxpayers, particularly homeowners, would have to make up the difference,” the report says. “That, in effect, would be an additional subsidy paid by people who live in Arlington Heights and potentially any other community that is home to a megaproject.”</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Closing of Oak Park's West Suburban Medical Center has triggered a legal battle among its owners
entries.summary: <p>The business partners who together bought West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park have now become legal foes, battling for control of the hospital in Cook County court.</p><p>Resilience Healthcare chief executive officer Manoj Prasad and the hospital’s landlord, Rathnakar Reddy Patlola, sued each other last month. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/22/west-suburban-medical-center-lawsuit-receiver-ramco-resilience-healthcare" target="_blank" >Patlola wants a judge</a> to appoint a receiver — a neutral third party — to help wrestle management of the hospital away from Prasad.</p><p>That request is before Cook County Circuit Judge Patrick Stanton, who said in court Wednesday that he hopes to rule by the end of the month.</p><p>Prasad abruptly closed the Oak Park institution in late March and furloughed most of its employees. He blamed the hospital’s electronic medical record system, which he said "never functioned correctly” for the payroll issues.</p><p>Prasad also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/08/08/weiss-memorial-hospital-emergency-room-in-uptown-closes" target="_blank" >shut down Weiss Memorial Hospital last summer</a> after the hospital in Uptown was stripped of Medicare and Medicaid funding.</p><p>That’s led to the court fight between Prasad and Patlola, with people on the West Side and in the near west suburbs having lost one of the few safety-net hospitals in that area. The remaining hospitals nearby — including Rush Oak Park Hospital, Loretto Hospital in Austin and Community First Medical Center in Portage Park — have been left to plug the gap. </p><h3></h3><h3>Who owns the hospitals? </h3><p>Patlola is a minority owner of Resilience Healthcare, which owns and operates West Suburban and Weiss Memorial.</p><p>Prasad is Resilience’s majority owner, in charge of day-to-day hospital operations.</p><p>But Patlola’s company Ramco is the sole owner of the land on which the hospitals sit. That includes West Suburban's Oak Park campus, its River Forest campus, Weiss and associated medical office buildings.</p><p>In 2022, the men together bought Weiss Memorial, West Suburban and West Suburban’s River Forest medical campus from Pipeline Health, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/6/8/23160414/state-board-approves-sale-of-weiss-memorial-hospital-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" >which had declared bankruptcy that year.</a></p><h3>What do the lawsuits say? </h3><p>Before suing for control of the hospitals, Patlola tried to oust Prasad and evict Resilience from both hospitals and the associated medical office buildings. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/14/west-suburban-medical-center-river-forest-campus-eviction-manoj-prasad" target="_blank" >Prasad then filed suit</a> against Patlola to stop the eviction.</p><p>In response, Patlola countersued, asking a judge to appoint a receiver to take control of West Suburban’s operations, allowing it to reopen.</p><p>In the lawsuit, Patlola accuses Prasad of “financial mismanagement and malfeasance.” The suit also seeks financial damages for back rent it says Prasad owes Patlola.</p><p>Patlola also accuses Prasad of having misused $35 million intended for hospital operations. The suit says Prasad moved the money to a separate bank account and “misappropriated” the funds for his “direct or indirect benefit.”</p><p>The lawsuit also accuses Prasad of breaching the hospitals’ leases and demands back rent of more than $24 million.</p><p>Prasad says that suit is “without merit" and that the hospitals’ leases bar Patlola from terminating the agreements or removing the hospital operator. He says the two men agreed to set rent for the hospital at just $1 a year until the operation shows a profit, which he says hasn't happened since they bought West Suburban and Weiss. </p><p>Prasad says the disputed millions went toward hospital payroll and operating expenses and that the money was transferred to a bank account tied to Westlaw Management Group that he says both men can access, though Patlola disputes that.</p><h3>What has happened in court? </h3><p>Lawyers for Prasad and Patlola have been arguing before Stanton about the financial details of Resilience Healthcare.</p><p>Both sides have agreed to have recently retired Judge Patrick Sherlock review years of bank records for several accounts tied to Resilience Healthcare and the hospitals.</p><p>Once Sherlock has turned over what he finds to Stanton, closing arguments are expected May 29.</p><p>Stanton will then decide whether to appoint a receiver to take temporary control of the business.</p><p>If Patlola wins, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/03/29/west-suburban-medical-center-owner-reopen-oak-park" target="_blank" >he’s in talks with Insight Hospital & Medical Center</a> to see whether that company could take over West Suburban. Insight’s CEO says the company is interested in helping reopen West Suburban.</p><p>Insight bought Mercy Hospital and Medical Center in Bronzeville after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2021/10/25/inside-the-fight-to-save-chicagos-historic-mercy-hospital" target="_blank" >it nearly closed in 2020</a>.</p><p>If Prasad keeps control, he has said he hopes to fully reopen the hospital by late June or early July. In the meantime, he has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/15/west-suburban-medical-center-reopening-some-clinics-amid-eviction-fight" target="_blank" >resumed some clinical services</a> at the Oak Park campus. </p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn
